translationRepairs: His grandson Sun Xingwu, a jinshi, rose to Vice Minister of Personnel.
His grandson Xingwu, a jinshi, rose to Vice Minister of Personnel.
After Wang Hongxu's biography, s0170 孫興吾 uses 孫 as kinship 'grandson,' not a surname; Xingwu is the given name. Removing false surname Sun is required and the proposed sentence is accurate.
His grandson Sun Xingwu, a jinshi, served as Vice Minister of Personnel.
His grandson Xingwu, a jinshi, served as Vice Minister of Personnel.
The literal field likewise misreads 孫 as surname Sun; the proposed 'His grandson Xingwu' correctly treats 孫 as kinship and 興吾 as the given name.

In time his followers multiplied; he founded a faction of his own. He bound Wang Hongxu to him as a die-hard ally, took He Kai, a supervising secretary, as a sworn brother, treated the Hanlin academician Chen Yuanlong as kinsman in a patron–nephew bond, and linked his children's marriages to Hongxu's elder brother Songling. All became his trusted agents, recruiting backers throughout the empire.

In time his followers multiplied; he founded a faction of his own. He bound Wang Hongxu to him as a die-hard ally, took He Kai, a supervising secretary, as a sworn brother, treated the Hanlin academician Chen Yuanlong as kinsman in a patron–nephew bond, and linked his children's marriages to Hongxu's elder brother Xuling. All became his trusted agents, recruiting backers throughout the empire.
s0210 names 鴻緒兄頊齡; 頊齡 is Xuling, not Songling. Replacing Songling with Xuling corrects the personal name while leaving the rest of the sentence intact.
In sum, Gao Shiqi, Wang Hongxu, Chen Yuanlong, He Kai, Wang Songling, and the rest have the nature of wolves, hearts of scorpions, and faces of ogres.
In sum, Gao Shiqi, Wang Hongxu, Chen Yuanlong, He Kai, Wang Xuling, and the rest have the nature of wolves, hearts of scorpions, and faces of ogres.
s0232 lists 王頊齡 among the impeached clique; the original Wang Songling misreads 頊齡, and Wang Xuling restores the correct name.
The historians observe: Scholar-officials who served directly in the inner court were called "study rooms," preserving the pre-conquest nomenclature.
The historians observe: When scholar-officials served on duty in the inner court, it was called the "Study," preserving the old name from before the conquest of the Pass.
In 儒臣直内廷，谓之「书房」, 谓之 names the duty/institution 书房, not the officials as 'study rooms.' The proposed idiomatic correctly makes the Study the referent and preserves 未入关前.
The historian comments: Confucian officials attending directly in the inner court are called "study rooms," preserving the old name from before entering the Pass.
The historian comments: When Confucian officials attend directly in the inner court, it is called the "Study," preserving the old name from before entering the Pass.

The original wrongly applies 「书房」 to the men; the proposal correctly retargets 谓之 to the service name but the bracketed '[this service]' is awkward editorial English. A clean clause with 'it is called the Study' fixes the referent without brackets.
The Southern Study with poetry, prose, calligraphy, and painting supplies the imperial—rank divided pure and urgent, participates in intimate counsel.
The Southern Study supplies poetry, prose, calligraphy, and painting for imperial use; its station is pure and close, and it takes part in confidential counsel.

The before literal garbles 供禦 and 地分淸切 into unintelligible English. The proposed rendering accurately gives imperial-use supply, a pure-and-close station, and participation in confidential counsel (參與密勿).
At first seeing Shiqi obtain ancient men's poetry and prose, one glance and he knew their period; in the heart taking it strange—not long, I too could do it.
At first, seeing Shiqi take up ancient poetry and prose and know their period at a glance, I thought it strange in my heart; before long, I too could do it.
得古人詩文 means handling/reading ancient poetry and prose, not obtaining 'ancient men's' writings; the proposed literal is grammatical and matches the Chinese sense of 一覽即知其時代 and 心以爲異.
Yet they leaned on power, formed factions, accepted bribes, and pursued private gain, and were impeached again and again; the Kangxi Emperor bent the law to preserve them.
Yet they leaned on power, formed factions, accepted bribes, and pursued private gain, and were impeached again and again; the Kangxi Emperor leniently preserved them.
曲予保全 means the emperor accommodated or leniently spared them; 'bent the law' invents a legal breach not stated in the Chinese. 'Leniently preserved' is accurate and natural.
